newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland says ECOFIN to further progress toward EMU.
newsitem.headline: Ireland says ECOFIN to further progress toward EMU.

text.p: An informal meeting of EU Finance ministers on Saturday will maintain momentum towards Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), according to Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, whose country is current EU president.

"This will be a work-in-progress meeting. I am not expecting any dramatic or earth-shattering announcements to come out of it," Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn told a news conference late on Tuesday.
"I am not expecting problems nor am I expecting a dramatic proclamation other than to say we made good progress and are on target for December," Quinn said.
The finance and economic ministers are due to submit a detailed report on EMU to a Dublin summit of EU government leaders in December.
Quinn said the first item for discussion at Saturday's meeting was the relationship between the currencies which initially join EMU and those which do not, the so-called 'ins' and 'outs'.
Ministers will then deal with the legal framework for the proposed euro single currency followed by detailed discussion on a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline after currency union.
They will also receive a report from the EU Commission on the European economy which should indicate that it is moving in "a positive and upward direction", Quinn said.
The Irish, keen and committed Europeans, are particularly interested in the relationship between the euro and those currencies which remain outside it.
Ireland is well on track to qualify for EMU but Britain's reservations about proceeding to a single currency remain a worry for its smaller neighbour.
Some 30 percent of Irish exports are still destined for Britain with employment-intensive domestic industry, rather than the multinational sector, particularly dependent on this trade.
These close trading ties with Britain make Ireland particularly vulnerable to a competitive devaluation of sterling if, as expected, Britain does not adopt the euro.
Quinn said the relationship between the 'ins' and 'outs' was not Ireland's exclusive concern but was high on its agenda.

"We have a vested interest in ensuring EMU works effectively and efficiently and especially the exchange rate mechanism with relation to sterling operates efficiently and effectively," he told reporters.

Ireland already meets the Maastricht criteria for membership of EMU and the Irish government is committed to keeping the public finances and inflation under control and maintaining a firm currency policy going into 1997, the qualifying year for the single currency project.

Irish inflation, as measured by the EU interim index of consumer prices, grew at a rate of 2.2 percent in the year to mid-August, while its debt/GDP ratio, on a Maastricht basis, is expected to fall to 76 percent by end-1996 from 81.5 percent at the end of 1995.
Although it remains above the 60 percent required by the treaty, Maastricht allows for a higher ratio if it "is sufficiently diminishing and approaching the reference value at a satisfactory pace".
Ireland's public deficit is below three percent of GDP, interest rates are low and the punt trades comfortably within its ERM bands. REUTER
